statement: Default to traditional periodization (base, build, specific, taper) with a hard day-easy day weekly pattern; do not default to reverse periodization, which showed no advantage, and offer it only as a user-selected option with no benefit claimed.
appliesTo: All distances from 5 km to 100 miles; recreational and trained runners

statement: Offer block periodization (a 1-2 week concentrated intensity block followed by lower-intensity weeks) only as an opt-in, flagged-experimental mode for trained athletes; block lengths are design choices, not evidence-derived.
appliesTo: Trained or well-trained runners with limited weekly time; not novices

statement: Allow at least 48 h between a high-intensity session and the next hard session; 24-48 h after threshold-intensity work; no spacing needed after easy running. Use the 48 h end for novices or when readiness is low. Evidence reflects autonomic recovery only; it does not cover recovery after a race (see the periodization-post-race rules).
appliesTo: All runners; fitter athletes may use the shorter end

statement: Default to 1-2 quality sessions per week for recreational runners with all other running easy; elite descriptive data show roughly one threshold and one speed session weekly but do not establish this number for recreational or ultra runners.
appliesTo: Recreational runners; lower end for novices and ultra goals

statement: Use a mostly pyramidal intensity distribution in base and build; for 5-10 km goals allow a shift toward polarized work in the final specific phase; keep marathon and longer pyramidal (extrapolated beyond marathon).
value: pyramidal base/build; optional polarized final specific phase for 5-10 km
appliesTo: Distance runners; evidence from highly trained and elite runners

statement: No study compares 3:1 with 2:1 cycles. Default to 3 build weeks plus 1 recovery week, and use 2:1 for novices, post-injury returns or when a fatigue flag is active (age alone does not select 2:1, per E3). These are conventions, not evidence-based values.
appliesTo: All runners

statement: Reduce volume in a planned recovery week by about 20-30% while keeping some intensity and frequency; this magnitude is not empirically derived.
appliesTo: All runners; larger reduction when a fatigue flag is active

statement: Insert or extend an unplanned recovery week only when at least two independent signals agree (subjective fatigue/readiness decline, submaximal efficiency decline, sleep-efficiency drop), sustained over several days; a single signal only trims the next hard session. The sustain duration (default 7 days) is a design choice.
appliesTo: All runners with check-in and wearable data

statement: Collect a brief subjective check-in (fatigue, sleep, soreness, mood, readiness, illness, pain) as a first-class load-adjustment input, weighted at least equal to wearable-derived metrics; do not use mood questionnaires alone to separate overreaching from ordinary fatigue. After a race a normal check-in is not evidence of muscle recovery (soreness and fatigue cleared by day 5 after 161 km while 400 m speed was still 12% slower), so it can delay but never shorten a post-race return.
value: daily or per run; daily throughout a post-race window
appliesTo: All runners

statement: Track a standardized submaximal efficiency index (pace at fixed HR, or HR at fixed pace, plus HR recovery) and RPE across weeks; a sustained efficiency fall with rising RPE is an overreaching signal, while a rising index across weeks indicates positive adaptation. Thresholds must be athlete-relative and are not validated.
appliesTo: Runners with HR and pace data

statement: Never use resting HRV, post-exercise HRV or HR recovery alone to trigger or clear a recovery week, to declare good adaptation, or to shorten or advance a post-race return; they rise in both adaptation and overreaching, and after a 100-mile race 24 h HRV was still depressed at 1 week and tracks autonomic state rather than muscle damage. Do not use VO2max estimates for overreaching detection.
appliesTo: All runners using wearable HRV or HRR

statement: Treat a sustained drop of about 2 percentage points in wearable sleep efficiency versus the athlete's own baseline during a heavy block as one supporting overreaching signal, never a standalone trigger. Wearable accuracy was not assessed in the source.
appliesTo: Runners with wearable sleep data, during heavy blocks

statement: Cap non-recovery-week increases in weekly running distance at about 10% as a conservative default (design choice) and never exceed 30%; the only direct evidence is an exploratory, non-significant novice-runner association. Do not claim injury prevention, and do not use ACWR bands as hard rules; display ACWR only as a descriptive metric if at all. Post-race return steps are a return to an established base and are exempt from the ramp, like the restart floor, but not from the session spike guard.
appliesTo: Novice and recreational runners; ultra build phases not covered

statement: Compute weekly load, monotony (mean daily load / SD) and strain (load x monotony) from session RPE x duration, show them descriptively, and flag only when an athlete's own strain exceeds their personal historical range; keep daily load varied. No universal thresholds exist.
appliesTo: Runners logging session RPE or an HR-derived load proxy

statement: Use three states (normal, possible accumulated fatigue, persistent suppression); never output an OTS or NFOR diagnosis; allow a deliberate overreach block only when no flag is active; when suppression persists for about 4 weeks (design choice, borrowed from the OTS review criterion) or illness-like symptoms accompany it, prompt a medical review that mentions illness, under-fuelling and iron status.
appliesTo: All runners

statement: Count the post-race window in days from the race (day 0), not in Monday plan weeks; days left in the race week belong to the hold. The window has three stages: a hold without running, 7-day steps of easy running at fractions of the pre-taper reference week, then the normal plan restarted through J7 with the hold length as the layoff.
appliesTo: Every goal race

statement: After a marathon-class race (32-42.2 km): no running on days 0-1; from day 2 (at least 48 h after the finish), up to 3 easy runs in the first 7-day step, on non-consecutive days, each at most 40 min at or below first-threshold heart rate (Z1, conversational). Easy running at this dose did not slow CK or LDH recovery and improved squat-jump recovery at 96 h against rest. The step volume fractions (0.5 then 0.75 of the reference week) are defaults.
value: 2 days hold; first step at most 3 runs of at most 40 min
appliesTo: Marathon-class races; recreational runners finishing in about 3-4 h (RCT population)

statement: Hold running after an ultra for 4 days (50 km class, above 42.2 to 80.5 km), 7 days (100 km class, to 130 km), 10 days (100-mile class, to 170 km) or 14 days (beyond 170 km). These are defaults: the 100-mile value follows the one-day-per-10-miles convention and sits inside the measured time course (neuromuscular function mostly back by day 9, fully by day 16 after 166 km; 400 m speed still 12% down at day 5 after 161 km); damage did not scale with distance up to 330 km, so the 14-day value for longer events is a judgement cap. Walking and light cross-training are allowed during the hold.
appliesTo: Ultra goal races by D1 class

statement: During the hold, walking and light non-impact activity are allowed and need not be planned; light activity in the week after a 118 km mountain race was not linked to worse marker recovery (observational), and elliptical work did not slow recovery after a marathon.
appliesTo: All post-race holds

statement: After the hold, return through 7-day steps of easy running capped at fractions of the pre-taper reference week: 0.5 then 0.75 for marathon and 50 km classes; 0.25, 0.5 then 0.75 for the 100 km class and longer. Run caps: first step at most 3 runs on non-consecutive days, each at most 40 min, no gain target; second step runs at most 60 min, short uphills allowed; later steps longest run at most 90 min. All running in Z1. Races of 5 km to half marathon keep the existing single 7-day step at 0.5. Fractions and caps are defaults except the marathon first step (see periodization-post-race-marathon-return).
unit: fraction of reference week; min per run
appliesTo: Marathon and ultra goal races

statement: Plan no intervals, threshold, race-pace, strides, plyometric or downhill sessions until every return step has ended (marathon from day 16, 50 km class day 18, 100 km class day 28, 100 miles day 31, beyond day 35, later with modifiers or gate extensions). Speed and jump power recover more slowly than soreness and aerobic capacity, CRP stays raised beyond 8 days after a marathon, and eccentric load drives damage.
value: no quality until the steps end
appliesTo: Marathon and ultra goal races

statement: Multiply the hold by 1.5, rounded up, once (not cumulatively) when any of these applies: the race descended at least 30 m per km, the runner is 40 or older, or the race history shows no earlier finish in this distance class. Eccentric load, masters age and first-time 100-mile racing go with slower or riskier recovery; the threshold and multiplier are defaults.
value: 1.5 (descent >= 30 m/km, age >= 40, first finish in class)
appliesTo: Marathon and ultra goal races

statement: In the post-race window, check-ins can only delay the return. A stage (hold to first step, step to step, last step to the normal plan) advances only when the last 2 check-ins before the boundary are not poor and report no pain or illness; otherwise the boundary moves one day at a time. A normal check-in never shortens the hold or skips a step. Without ratings the default schedule runs unchanged and the app says that ratings are needed for adjustments. After 14 days of extension, show the J8 clinician checklist. The direction (subjective measures first, delay only) is grade B; the count of 2 and the 14 days are defaults, so the parameters carry grade D.
appliesTo: All post-race windows; runners who rate

statement: When the runner has at least 14 check-ins in the 28 days before the race, a post-race check-in is also poor when it is worse than the runner's own pre-race median by the J2 margin; a check-in poor by either the fixed scale or the own baseline counts as poor, so the comparison can only add caution. The direction is grade C; the count of 14 is a default, so the parameter carries grade D.
unit: check-ins in the 28 days before the race
appliesTo: Runners with a pre-race check-in history

statement: HRV and resting HR keep their J3 and J4 roles in the post-race window: they can delay a run or a stage, never advance one. Expect HRV below baseline for more than a week after a 100-mile race and say so; do not treat HRV as a measure of muscle recovery.
appliesTo: Runners with wearable HRV or resting HR

statement: Ask about pain and illness daily through the post-race window. Pain that changes gait or focal bone pain applies red flags n1/n2 and holds the current stage; illness applies n3. Do not lengthen holds on immune 'open window' grounds; a runner who reported illness in the 3 weeks before the race gets caution copy (post-race infection 33% vs 16%).
value: n1-n3 apply; caution copy after pre-race illness
appliesTo: All post-race windows

statement: A completed race of marathon distance or longer (42.195 km or more) does not count toward the 30-day reference, in the check and in the generator alike; shorter races count as runs. Otherwise a 100-mile finish would allow training runs up to 1.10 times the race. The reference falls back to the longest remaining completed run of the 30 days.
value: races of 42.195 km or more excluded from the 30-day reference
appliesTo: The G-1 check and the generator, after a marathon or longer race
